mappings.note: POOR FIT. The load is found from VR and EFFICIENCY, neither of which exists in curriculum 82; only the block-and-tackle identification (LO-3), the labelled diagram (C8.1) and the load/effort idea (C2.6) are covered.
Crowbar arm ratio 3:1 converted straight into a load/effort ratio - a mechanical-advantage calculation (C2.6 only) on a lever (LO-3). Not an energy item: no work or energy quantity appears anywhere.

Parts 1 to 3 trace PE becoming KE as the stone rolls down (LO-7); part 4 asks whether the conservation law still holds once friction is admitted, which is C-2.6-LO-1 and the only part not covered by LO-7.

Three separable demands: define power and its SI unit (C-2.6-LO-1), say which form the electrical energy becomes (LO-5), and compare the two pumps' power numerically (C-2.6-LO-2). The equal-work observation rides on the power definition.

Half-way-down KE can only be got by conservation during free fall (LO-7), with mgh and the energy values computed (LO-6). The stem names conservation of mechanical energy but asks for values, so LO-7 leads over C-2.6-LO-1.
WEAK FIT. Both parts run on E = P x t (C-2.6-LO-2), but the item is really about converting 'units' to joules; the kilowatt-hour has no outcome in curriculum 82.

Three of the four scenes are zero-work cases decided from the definition - no displacement, then a perpendicular carry (LO-1) - while the chair gives one 50 N x 2 m calculation (LO-2). Both outcomes are separately marked.

Parts 1, 2 and 4 are the definition and its two conditions (LO-1); part 3 asks where Rohan's expended energy went, which needs the muscular-to-thermal conversion (LO-5). That third part is what separates it from the other wall-pushing items.

Positive work by the striker and negative work by the keeper are sign judgements from the definition (LO-1); the stated 0.2 m hand displacement makes the keeper's work a computable quantity (LO-2). The MCQ version gives no distance and so stops at LO-1.
Part (a) defines kinetic energy (LO-5); parts (b) and (c) compare the two cars and quantify the effect of doubling Car A's speed (LO-6). Definition plus calculation, so both siblings are cited.

Lifting work is computed (LO-2), the horizontal carry is zero work against gravity by the definition (LO-1), and the last part asks which FORM of energy the suitcase gains (LO-5). Three parts, three different outcomes.

Names elastic PE and how the work stores it (LO-5), tracks its release into the arrow's KE (LO-7), and finishes with an mgh value for the 0.05 kg arrow at 2 m (LO-6). The numerical tail is what distinguishes it from the other archery case study.

The same bow story as C182 but with no numbers: naming the stored form (LO-5) and the PE-to-KE release, including how more stretch means more energy and speed (LO-7). No LO-6 precisely because nothing is evaluated.

Part (a) defines mechanical energy as KE plus PE (LO-5); the rest tracks the swap between them down the roller-coaster drop (LO-7). Friction is declared negligible, so the conservation-law code C-2.6-LO-1 is not the discriminator.

Parts 1 and 2 compute work as weight times height (LO-2), part 3 computes and compares power (C-2.6-LO-2), and part 4 asks the SI unit of power (C-2.6-LO-1). Each part sits on a different outcome, which is why all three are cited.

Part (a) asks for the STATEMENT of the work-energy theorem (LO-3), then the KE values are computed and the braking work read off as their change (LO-6). The explicit 'state the theorem' is what makes LO-3 primary rather than incidental.

Four sub-parts that build one argument: force radial, displacement tangential, angle 90 degrees, work zero. All of it is the perpendicular clause of the work definition, LO-1, and nothing is computed, so LO-2 stays out.

Requires naming two machines from their descriptions - fixed pulley on the flagpole, movable pulley on the load (LO-3) - and comparing what each does to the effort, i.e. mechanical advantage (C2.6). The identification half is unusually well covered by this frame.

PARTLY UNCOVERED. Parts (i) and (ii) are MA = L/h and the effort, reachable only through C2.6, with LO-3 for the inclined plane; part (iii) is answered with efficiency and velocity ratio, neither of which any code in this frame names.

Identifies the ramp as an inclined plane (LO-3), computes its MA (C2.6), and then explains the force-over-distance trade-off at constant work, which rests on the definition of work (LO-1). Three demands, three codes.

PARTIAL FIT. Identifying the fulcrum and the lever is LO-3 and the moment balance that seats Meera is C2.6, but the demand to name the lever CLASS has no outcome - lever classes are absent from curriculum 82.

Parts 1, 2 and 4 are KE evaluations including the doubling effect (LO-6); part 3 gets the braking work as the change in KE, which is the work-energy theorem (LO-3). LO-6 leads here because three of four parts are evaluations, the reverse of case study C186.

Parts 1, 2 and 4 are the free-fall PE/KE exchange with values (LO-7 plus LO-6), while part 3 explicitly invokes the LAW of conservation of energy for the constant sum (C-2.6-LO-1). All three are separately marked.

Parts 1 and 2 ask what a 100 W rating MEANS, i.e. the definition of the watt (C-2.6-LO-1); parts 3 and 4 compute energy over 5 hours and convert a kWh (C-2.6-LO-2, with the commercial unit itself uncovered by the frame).

POOR FIT. Only parts (i) and (ii), the mechanical advantage and whether it suffices, are reachable, and only through the competency C2.6; parts (iii) velocity ratio and (iv) efficiency have no code at all. LO-3 covers the lever itself.
